items.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023
items.q: But you know after the sixties and Coltrane and everybody there was only so much you could do to do something new. He had extended the harmony and extended the rhythm as far as you can

ctx.x: You did. I have some quotes here. But if jazz was in trouble forty years ago, where is it now?

Well you know there’s a lot of discussion about that today. And it centers on the fact that we have so many people learning it in academic situations and what’s the impact of that? I mean and that goes right to the question of style, where does style come from? You know almost everybody, when they get down to it, will say that style comes from how you recover from what you perceive to be as mistakes. They’re not mistakes, they’re opportunities. And it’s in the recovery of playing something you didn’t intend or…

something to do with being a sideman and learning out on the road and being on a bus with other musicians. It has something to do with the grit that was in the music that tends not to be in the music that way anymore because well it’s often said, if you spend eight hours a day in a practice room, you’re going to sound like you’re in a practice room. If you spend eight hours a day hanging out with musicians and riding on the bus like they used to do, that’s going to affect how you sound as well. So I wouldn’t say…
